name: fasm2-studio
description: Syntax highlighting, autocomplete, hover docs, cross-file navigation, live diagnostics, build tasks, and real gdb-based debugging (experimental lldb-mi on macOS) for flat assembler 2 (fasmg), compatible with classic flat assembler 1 sources.

enumDescriptions: flat assembler 2 / fasmg. Also the right answer for a bare fasmg project.
Classic flat assembler 1. Choose this for a project fasm1 builds, since its syntax is not auto-detected.
fasm2Studio.defaultDialect.description: Dialect assumed for source files where the dialect cannot be auto-detected from their contents. Scoped per folder, so a workspace holding both a fasm1 and a fasm2 project can give each the right answer.

fasm2Studio.fasm2CompilerPath.description: Path to the fasm2/fasmg executable. Leave empty to auto-detect it on PATH.

fasm2Studio.fasm1CompilerPath.description: Path to the fasm1 (classic flat assembler) executable. Leave empty to auto-detect it on PATH.

fasm2Studio.diagnosticsEnabled.description: Compile in the background to show errors/warnings as you edit.

fasm2Studio.diagnosticsDebounceMs.description: Milliseconds to wait after you stop typing before re-running diagnostics.

fasm2Studio.buildOutputPath.markdownDescription: Output path for Build/Run/Debug, relative to the source file's directory (e.g. `../bin/cc` to keep build output out of the source tree). `FASM: Debug`'s `.lst` listing is placed alongside it. Leave empty to use the source file name with its extension stripped, next to the source.

fasm2Studio.includePath.markdownDescription: Semicolon-separated list of extra directories to search for a bare `include 'foo.inc'` that isn't found next to the including file, passed as the compiler's `INCLUDE` environment variable. Many real fasmg projects need this to build at all (e.g. fasmg's own Windows examples require setting it to their `include` package directory, exactly as their bundled `make.bat` does with `set include=...`). Leave empty to only use whatever `INCLUDE` (if any) your system environment already provides.

fasm2Studio.fasm2Preload.markdownDescription: Include file assembled before the source itself (via fasmg's `-i` flag), for projects whose instruction set is preloaded by a wrapper script rather than written in the source. `fasm2` is only `fasmg` plus a wrapper that preloads the x86 package this way, and instruction-set ports commonly ship the same arrangement. Set this together with `#fasm2Studio.includePath#` and the language server follows the preload too — giving hover, completion and go-to-definition for that instruction set, and letting it tell a non-x86 project from an x86 one. Nothing here is x86-specific: it will load a 68000 or Z80 instruction set just as readily. Use `fasm2.inc`, with `#fasm2Studio.includePath#` pointing at fasm2's `include` directory, to drive a bare `fasmg` binary as if it were `fasm2`. Leave empty for a normal `fasm2` install.

fasm2Studio.compilerArgs.markdownDescription: Extra command-line arguments for the assembler, used by everything that runs it: Build, Run, Debug, and the background compile behind live error checking. Some projects do not assemble without one — fasmg gives up after 100 passes, which a macro-heavy project genuinely exceeds (`["-p", "300"]`), and a build-time definition is supplied as `["-i", "define TARGET_LINUX 1"]`, since fasmg has no `-d` the way fasm1 does. Each entry is one argument and is quoted as written, so a value containing a space stays a single argument. They are passed after `#fasm2Studio.fasm2Preload#` and before the listing macro a debug build injects, and fasmg takes the last occurrence of a repeated flag, so a flag set here overrides the same flag set by this extension.

markdownEnumDescriptions: Ask before rewriting anything, showing how many paths in how many files would change.
Rewrite the affected `include` paths without asking.
Leave `include` paths alone; renaming a file that others include will break their paths.
fasm2Studio.updateIncludesOnFileMove.markdownDescription: Keeps `include` paths pointing at the right file when you rename or move one in the explorer — both the paths that named the moved file and the moved file's own relative paths, which are now resolved from a different directory. fasm has no module system, so a path in a string literal is the only thing tying two files together, and nothing about a stale one looks wrong until the assembler fails on it.

fasm2Studio.codeLens.markdownDescription: Shows Run / Debug / Build actions above the `format` directive of a file that is a program in its own right. Only entry points get them: an included fragment builds through whichever program includes it, which is not something a lens on the fragment could name. Needs the language server, since which files are entry points is read from the same include graph that go-to-definition uses.

markdownEnumDescriptions: The address each instruction is assembled at.
How many bytes each instruction encodes to.
The machine code each instruction encodes to, as `B8 3C 00 00 00`.
fasm2Studio.inlayHints.markdownDescription: Annotates each line that produces machine code with where it lands in memory, how large it is, and the bytes it encodes to — the information you would otherwise have to build and read a `.lst` file to see. The byte modes show the encoding itself, which is the thing a `.lst` is usually opened for; an encoding longer than 16 bytes (a `format` directive emitting a whole ELF header, a `db` of a string) is elided inline, and every hint carries its full dump as a tooltip whatever the mode. The data comes from the same background compile that live error checking already runs, so this needs `#fasm2Studio.diagnosticsEnabled#`, a trusted workspace, and a fasm2/fasmg project (fasm1's listing format is not supported). Off by default: it annotates most lines of a typical file, and generating the listing adds a little to every background compile.

fasm2Studio.runArgs.markdownDescription: Command-line arguments passed to your program by `FASM: Run` and `FASM: Build and Run`. Each entry is one argument and is quoted as written, so a value containing a space stays a single argument rather than being split by the shell. The debugger has taken these since launch configurations existed (`args` in `launch.json`); this is the same thing for the two commands that run the program without one.

fasm2Studio.gdbPath.markdownDescription: Path to the MI-speaking debugger used by `FASM: Debug` — `gdb` on Linux/Windows, `lldb-mi` on macOS. Leave empty to use `gdb` from `PATH` (`lldb-mi` on macOS; e.g. gdb from MSYS2/MinGW-w64 on Windows, or your distro's package on Linux).

fasm2Studio.format.mnemonicColumn.description: Column (0-based) that Format Document aligns instruction mnemonics to, measured from the current indent. 0 leaves mnemonics unaligned.

fasm2Studio.format.operandColumn.description: Column (0-based) that Format Document aligns operands to, measured from the current indent. 0 leaves a single space after the mnemonic.

fasm2Studio.format.commentColumn.markdownDescription: Absolute column that Format Document aligns trailing `;` comments to. 0 aligns each run of commented lines to a column of its own instead: the column you aligned them to is kept whenever it still clears the code, and only moves to the next tab stop past the longest line in the run when the code has outgrown it.

enumDescriptions: Log each request/notification the editor and the language server exchange.
Log each message together with its full JSON payload.
fasm2Studio.trace.server.description: Logs the traffic between VS Code and the FASM language server into its output channel. Turn this on when reporting a bug about hover, completion, navigation or live error checking not working — without it there is nothing to attach.

viewsWelcome.contents:
No file here declares a `format` directive, so this workspace has no program to build yet.

A file becomes an entry point by naming the output it produces (`format ELF64 executable 3`, `format PE64 console`, `format binary`). An included fragment doesn't need one — it builds through whichever program includes it.
[Create a Program](command:fasm2Studio.newFile)

Already have one? It may not be indexed yet.
[Refresh](command:fasm2Studio.entryPoints.refresh)

file.description: Source file to assemble, relative to the workspace or absolute.

output.description: Output file path. Defaults to the source file name with its extension stripped.

dialect.description: Overrides auto-detected dialect for this task.

extraArgs.description: Additional command-line arguments passed to the compiler.

debugBuild.description: Injects the bundled listing macro (fasm2 only) so the FASM debugger can map addresses back to source lines.

program.description: Path to the assembled executable. Defaults to the source file name with its extension stripped.

listingFile.description: Path to the .lst listing produced by a debug build. Defaults to "<program>.lst".

gdbPath.description: Path to gdb (or lldb-mi on macOS). Leave unset to use "gdb" from PATH ("lldb-mi" on macOS).

cwd.description: Working directory for the debugged program.

stopOnEntry.description: Stop at the program's first instruction.

reverseDebugging.description: Record execution so the program can be stepped backwards — Step Back and Reverse Continue, for answering "what was in that register before I clobbered it" without restarting. Costs a lot of speed: gdb single-steps the program and journals every register and memory write, so leave it off for ordinary runs. Requires gdb (lldb-mi on macOS has no execution recording), and implies stopOnEntry, since recording has to begin before your code runs.

args.description: Command-line arguments passed to the debugged program.

enumDescriptions: A terminal in the panel. The program can be typed into as well as read.
A separate terminal window, for a program that wants the whole screen to itself.
The Debug Console. Output only — a program that reads stdin will wait forever.
console.description: Where the debugged program's own input and output go. Only a terminal can carry input, so a program that reads stdin needs one; the Debug Console can show output but has nothing to type into. On Windows a terminal setting gives the program its own console window instead, since there is no pty for gdb to share.

env.description: Environment variables for the debugged program, merged over the inherited environment.

stackWords.description: How many machine words at and above the stack pointer the Registers panel's Stack group lists. The whole group is one memory read however deep it goes, so raise it freely for code with deep frames.

stackRedZone.description: Also list the 128 bytes below the stack pointer — the System V red zone, which a leaf routine may use as scratch without moving rsp. Off by default because for most code those words are leftovers rather than data; on when you are debugging a leaf that uses them, where nothing else shows them.

asmFile.description: The .asm source file the program was built from. Its listing is what maps addresses back to source lines.

processId.description: Process to attach to. Leave the default to pick one from a list. On Linux, attaching to a process this editor did not start requires /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope to be 0 — gdb says so plainly if it isn't.

coreFile.description: A core dump to open instead of attaching to a running process. Registers, memory and the faulting source line are all readable; nothing can be resumed or stepped.

program.description: Path to the assembled executable the process is running (or that produced the core). Defaults to the source file name with its extension stripped.

listingFile.description: Path to the .lst listing from the build that produced this exact binary. Defaults to "<program>.lst".

gdbPath.description: Path to gdb (or lldb-mi on macOS). Leave unset to use "gdb" from PATH ("lldb-mi" on macOS).

stackWords.description: How many machine words at and above the stack pointer the Registers panel's Stack group lists. The whole group is one memory read however deep it goes, so raise it freely for code with deep frames.

stackRedZone.description: Also list the 128 bytes below the stack pointer — the System V red zone, which a leaf routine may use as scratch without moving rsp. Off by default because for most code those words are leftovers rather than data; on when you are debugging a leaf that uses them, where nothing else shows them.

walkthroughs.title: Get started with FASM2 Studio
walkthroughs.description: This extension drives the assembler and debugger you already have installed — it does not bundle either. Three steps to a program you can build, run and step through.

steps.title: Install an assembler
steps.description:
FASM2 Studio needs `fasm2` (flat assembler g) and/or `fasm1` on your PATH.

Linux/macOS: [download one from flatassembler.net](https://flatassembler.net/download.php) and put the binary somewhere on PATH, such as `~/.local/bin`.
Windows: the official fasm2 distribution ships a `fasm2.cmd` wrapper — add its folder to PATH.

Already installed somewhere unusual? Point at it directly instead.
[Select Compiler](command:fasm2Studio.selectCompiler)

steps.title: Tell it which dialect your project is
steps.description:
fasm2 is detected automatically. **fasm1 is not** — the syntax that would identify it is also valid fasmg, so a fasm1 project silently falls back to the fasm2 default and reports errors on code that assembles perfectly.

If your project is fasm1, say so once and it is written into the project's own settings.
[Select Dialect](command:fasm2Studio.selectDialect)

steps.title: Build and run
steps.description:
Open a `.asm` file and use the ▷ button in the editor title bar, or the command palette.

Don't have one yet? Create a hello world that already builds and runs — pick your platform and it writes the `format` line, the entry point and the exit for you.

Included fragments are handled for you: building an `.inc` with no `format` of its own assembles the real entry point that includes it.
[New File](command:fasm2Studio.newFile)
[Build and Run](command:fasm2Studio.buildAndRun)

steps.title: Debug with real breakpoints
steps.description:
Debugging drives `gdb` (`lldb-mi` on macOS) against your assembled binary: breakpoints in your source, registers, memory, watchpoints and a disassembly view.

gdb is preinstalled on most Linux distributions. On Windows install it from MSYS2 or w64devkit.
[Start Debugging](command:fasm2Studio.debug)

steps.title: See the machine code inline
steps.description:
Every line that produces code can be annotated with the address it lands at and the bytes it encodes to — `mov eax, 60` alongside `B8 3C 00 00 00` — instead of building and reading a `.lst` file.

It rides on the background compile that live error checking already runs, so it costs no second pass. Off by default, since it annotates most lines of a typical file.
[Annotate Instructions Inline](command:fasm2Studio.selectInlayHints)

untrustedWorkspaces.description: Reading code is safe here and stays fully enabled: syntax highlighting, hover, completion, navigation, folding and formatting all work, since none of them run anything. What is withheld is everything that starts a process — live error checking, Build, Run and Debug — because those would execute an assembler (and gdb) against source the workspace controls. The six settings listed above are ignored while the workspace is untrusted, so a cloned repo cannot choose the binary that runs or the arguments it runs with; trusting the folder restores both them and the disabled features.

virtualWorkspaces.description: Diagnostics, build, run and debug all spawn real processes against real files on disk, which a virtual filesystem cannot provide.
